Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Cross-frequency synchronization connects networks of fast and slow oscillations during visual working memory maintenance" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by David Van Essen (Senior editor), Maurizio Corbetta (Reviewing editor), and three reviewers.

All reviewers found that the revised manuscript addresses most of their concerns.

I would ask you to consider Reviewer 2 comments on the SNR and description of Figure 7.

We hope that these issues can be dealt with expeditiously.

Reviewer #1:

In my opinion, the authors have done a fine job at addressing the Reviewers' concerns. In particular I appreciate the new cross-validation analyses.

Their new Hypothesis Figure 1 is very helpful, and is a useful addition overall.

I am in the awkward, but pleasant, position of not having any major questions or concerns.

Reviewer #2:

The authors have extensively revised the manuscript and included several new analyses. This has substantially strengthened the manuscript and most of my concerns have been addressed. Overall, this is a very good paper reporting several intriguing and novel results. However, two points remain:

1) I am concerned that the SNR confound analysis is based on the invalid assumption that only the measurement noise (assessed with an empty room measurement) constitutes noise in the present context of a potential SNR confound. In contrast, for this confound, also any neuronal signals not of interest (and likely without CFS) should be considered noise. In particular, this noise entails broad band (1/f) activity, which constitutes a major part of the measured neuronal signal. For any frequency band, the measured neuronal signal does not only reflect oscillatory and potentially CFS-coupled signals of interest, but typically even more strongly broad-band neuronal activity. Thus, the employed SNR estimates are likely grossly overestimated. In turn, the CFS effects predicted from amplitude changes are likely underestimated. In light of this consideration, the authors' statement that predicted and observed CFS effect were not correlated is particularly important, because this would provide evidence against an SNR confound irrespective of incorrect SNR estimates. I suggest to report corresponding statistics to substantiate this claim. Furthermore, it should be clarified why the analysis is restricted to 200 parcels with strongest CFS effects.

2) The description of the new Figures 7B/C seems misleading. My understanding is that the apparent match between 1:1 and CFS coupling (filling/border) is simply a necessity of the fact that only matching areas were plotted. E.g., there could not have been a region with a yellow filling and violet border in these plots. If this is indeed correct, it should be clearly stated that these figures are not used to assess the match between 1:1 and CFS networks, but merely to identify matching regions.

Reviewer #3:

The authors have responded to the comments as best as they could or were willing to (e.g., no new subjects tested). I don't see any major technical problems with the manuscript or the analyses.

My main concern is the same as with the initial submission: I'm just not sure what to make of the results. It's a bit of a "throw the spaghetti against the wall and see what sticks" approach. The brain is sufficiently complex that pretty much any all-to-all data analysis application will produce "stuff", some of which may be real and meaningful and some of which may be spurious or at least not generalizable. There are many publications in the literature that do massive all-to-all exploratory connectivity analyses, and it's never really clear what they mean, except to confirm that there are large-scale networks in the brain.

The authors' argument is that phase-amplitude coupling might not be fast enough for some of the faster aspects of cognition, and therefore the brain might be phase-phase synchronization (CFS). Fair enough, and it's hard to disagree with this claim. But I'm not sure that this experiment provides necessary evidence for this. Why does WM need to be fast? Why couldn't the brain use "slow" PAC here? (Does the brain even need PAC for WM?)

I think an important conceptual advance would come from showing that CFS "solves a problem" or at least correlates with task performance in a way that is unique amongst connectivity manifestations. Otherwise, this manuscript -- methodologically rigorous as it is -- seems to be just another example of how a massively complex system like the brain can be measured using many different analysis techniques.

I hope my comments are not interpreted as being too negative or critical. The authors clearly put a lot of work and careful thought into this manuscript. It just seems to me to be more a methodological exercise than a conceptual or theoretical advance. But that's just my opinion.

results.result: The manuscript reviews prior literature establishing that working memory has limited capacity (3-4 objects), involves sensory storage and executive control, and is supported by enhanced neuronal activity in visual and fronto-parietal areas during maintenance, with distinct functional roles for visual cortex (information maintenance) and lateral prefrontal cortex (attentional regulation).
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C7 are all supported by appropriate citations to prior literature and represent well-established background knowledge in the field. These claims provide the necessary context for the current study and are appropriately attributed to previous work.

results.result: Prior work has established that phase synchronization in beta and gamma bands supports integration of visual information during VWM, while high-alpha band synchronization in fronto-parietal areas supports attentional and executive control functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C12 are supported by citations to prior studies in both macaque recordings and human MEG/EEG. Claim C12 is an inference from anatomical patterns but is appropriately presented as a hypothesis rather than established fact.

results.result: Prior research has shown that beta and gamma oscillation amplitudes correlate positively with VWM performance and support content representation, while alpha oscillations show negative correlations with capacity and are stronger for distractors, suggesting theta/alpha oscillations underlie attentional functions by facilitating relevant and suppressing irrelevant information.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C18 are well-supported by citations to prior literature. These claims establish the functional roles of different frequency bands in VWM and provide the rationale for investigating cross-frequency coupling mechanisms.

results.result: The manuscript distinguishes between two forms of cross-frequency coupling: PAC (phase-amplitude coupling), which has been observed during VWM but cannot promote consistent spike-time relationships, and CFS (cross-frequency phase synchrony), which indicates direct phase coupling and could mechanistically support cross-frequency integration at the temporal resolution of the faster oscillation.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C24 are supported by appropriate citations and provide clear conceptual distinctions between PAC and CFS. The theoretical framework for why CFS might be functionally important (C21, C23) is logically sound and appropriately presented as a hypothesis.

results.result: Prior observations of CFS have been limited to sensor-level human studies (resting-state and VWM tasks), one intracranial EEG study in human hippocampus, and rat microcircuit studies, leaving the cortical sources and functional significance of CFS unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C31 are supported by appropriate citations and accurately characterize the limitations of prior CFS research (C28), which motivates the current study's source-localized approach.

results.result: The study found that CFS was load-dependently enhanced between theta and alpha-gamma oscillations and between alpha and beta-gamma oscillations during VWM maintenance among visual, fronto-parietal, and dorsal attention systems, connected hubs of within-frequency synchronized networks, and predicted individual VWM capacity.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35 represent the main findings of the study and are supported by the experimental data presented in multiple figures. These are the core results that the entire manuscript is built around.

results.result: Behavioral performance showed that hit rate decreased with VWM load but remained above chance for the highest load of six objects.
results.evaluation: Claim C36 is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1. This validates that the task was appropriately challenging and subjects were performing above chance across all load conditions.

results.result: Single-trial analysis demonstrated that CFS between middle frontal sulcus and occipital pole, as well as 1:1 synchronization in separate alpha and gamma networks, were strengthened during VWM retention.
results.evaluation: Claim C37 is supported by single-trial data shown in Figure 2d. This provides proof-of-principle that CFS can be observed at the single-trial level, strengthening the validity of the group-level findings.

results.result: CFS of low-theta and low-alpha oscillations with higher frequency bands was suppressed below baseline during VWM retention, while high-theta and high-alpha CFS was enhanced, showing that CFS is both up- and down-regulated dynamically. The harmonic consistency of CFS across frequency ratios was significant for enhanced high-theta and high-alpha bands and suppressed low-alpha band.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C44 are supported by data in Figure 3a-b with appropriate statistical testing (p < 0.05, FDR corrected). The harmonic consistency analysis provides strong evidence that the observed CFS reflects systematic phase coupling rather than spurious effects.

results.result: CFS between high-alpha-band consistent frequency pairs was positively correlated with memory load, theta-consistent CFS showed weak load-dependent modulations, and low-alpha consistent CFS was negatively correlated with VWM load.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 are supported by statistical analysis (Spearman's rank correlation, FDR corrected) and data shown in Figure 3c-d. The differential load effects across frequency bands suggest functionally distinct roles for different CFS networks.

results.result: Leave-one-out and effect size control analyses showed that the findings are robust despite the small sample size (N=12) and cannot be attributable to any single subject.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49 are supported by control analyses shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2. These analyses appropriately address concerns about the small sample size and demonstrate the robustness of the main findings.

results.result: Multiple control analyses demonstrated that the observed CFS effects cannot be explained by changes in signal-to-noise ratio, concurrent amplitude changes, or non-sinusoidal waveforms. The observed CFS changes were much larger than predicted by SNR changes, task effects on amplitudes explained little variance in CFS, and cross-frequency amplitude correlations showed patterns distinct from CFS.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C55 are supported by extensive control analyses shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 3-8. These controls are critical for establishing that CFS reflects true phase coupling rather than artifacts, and the analyses are thorough and appropriate.

results.result: Network visualization revealed that theta-consistent CFS networks had low-frequency hubs mainly in fronto-parietal and dorsal/ventral attention systems, with high-frequency hubs in dorsal attention, sensorimotor, and default-mode systems. High-alpha-consistent CFS networks showed low-frequency hubs in right-hemispheric fronto-parietal and default-mode systems strongly connected to gamma oscillations in visual cortex, with high-frequency gamma hubs in visual system connected to alpha oscillations in LPFC and posterior parietal cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C63 are supported by detailed network visualizations in Figure 4a-b and external source data. The anatomical localization of CFS hubs to task-relevant systems (visual, fronto-parietal, dorsal attention) is consistent with the hypothesized functional role of CFS in integrating sensory and attentional functions.

results.result: CFS connections between high-alpha and beta oscillations at 1:2 ratio were localized to sensorimotor, dorsal attention, and ventral attention systems, distinct from alpha:gamma CFS, suggesting functionally distinct forms of cross-frequency coupling.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 are supported by network visualization in Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The distinct anatomical patterns for alpha:beta versus alpha:gamma CFS support the inference that these may serve different functional roles.

results.result: Low-frequency and high-frequency hubs for low-alpha consistent CFS suppression were predominantly found in default-mode and sensorimotor systems that are putatively task-irrelevant in VWM.
results.evaluation: Claim C66 is supported by network visualization in Figure 4—figure supplement 2. This finding suggests that CFS suppression may reflect disengagement of task-irrelevant networks, complementing the enhancement of CFS in task-relevant networks.

results.result: In the Load condition, high-alpha low-frequency hubs were found in left-hemispheric visual system, right-hemispheric fronto-parietal areas, and sensorimotor regions bilaterally, with high-frequency gamma hubs overlapping in visual system and right-hemispheric middle frontal gyrus and superior parietal gyrus.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 are supported by network visualization in Figure 5. The Load condition results show how CFS networks are modulated by task demands, with some overlap but also differences from the Mean condition networks.

results.result: System-level connectivity analysis showed that VWM retention was associated with significantly denser CFS coupling of theta-oscillations in multiple systems with alpha-gamma oscillations in sensorimotor and dorsal attention systems, high-alpha oscillations synchronized with gamma within and between dorsal attention, visual, sensorimotor, and fronto-parietal systems, with different patterns in Mean versus Load conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C74 are supported by system-level connectivity analysis in Figure 6 with appropriate statistical testing against randomized data. This analysis complements the detailed network visualizations and confirms the main patterns at a coarser anatomical scale.

results.result: CFS hubs were significantly co-localized with hubs of within-frequency (1:1) synchronized networks. Low-frequency CFS hubs showed strong correlations with slow 1:1 network hubs, while high-frequency CFS hubs showed weaker but significant correlations with fast 1:1 network hubs. Shared hubs in both 1:1 and CFS networks were identified in fronto-parietal and dorsal attention systems for alpha networks and in visual system for gamma networks.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C81 are supported by correlation analysis in Figure 7a and network visualizations in Figure 7b-c. This is a critical finding that supports the hypothesis that CFS connects within-frequency synchronized networks, and the statistical evidence is appropriate (p < 0.05, corrected).

results.result: PAC analysis revealed that theta and low-alpha band phases were coupled with alpha and beta band amplitudes at 1:2 ratio, with weak theta:gamma PAC at higher ratios. Importantly, PAC was suppressed in the high-alpha band where prominent CFS was observed, demonstrating that PAC and CFS are clearly distinct phenomena.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 are supported by PAC analysis in Figure 8. The distinct patterns of PAC versus CFS, particularly the suppression of PAC where CFS is enhanced, provide strong evidence that these are functionally different forms of cross-frequency coupling.

results.result: The strength of high-alpha consistent CFS networks at low ratios (1:2-1:5) predicted individual VWM capacity (r=0.343, p=0.003), while high-theta consistent CFS at high ratios (1:6-1:9) was correlated with individual capacity (r=0.376, p=0.001). Both high-alpha:beta and high-alpha:low-gamma CFS were significantly correlated with VWM capacity.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 are supported by correlation analysis in Figure 9a with appropriate statistics (Pearson correlation, FDR corrected). This is a critical finding demonstrating the functional significance of CFS, as individual differences in CFS strength predict behavioral performance.

results.result: PAC network strength showed no significant correlations with individual VWM capacity after correction for multiple comparisons, indicating that cortical CFS is functionally significant in human VWM maintenance and that CFS and PAC are functionally distinct phenomena.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C91 are supported by correlation analysis in Figure 9c-d. The lack of behavioral correlation for PAC contrasts with the significant correlations for CFS, providing strong evidence for the functional distinctiveness and behavioral relevance of CFS specifically.

results.result: The study demonstrates that CFS connects slow and fast cortical oscillations across visual, fronto-parietal, and dorsal attention systems during VWM retention, is dynamically regulated and correlated with task demands, predicts individual VWM capacity, and may serve as a mechanism for coordinating neuronal processing and regulating communication among oscillatory networks at different frequencies.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C95 represent the main conclusions of the study and are well-supported by the comprehensive set of findings presented throughout the manuscript. The evidence includes task-related modulation, load-dependent effects, anatomical localization to task-relevant systems, co-localization with 1:1 network hubs, and behavioral correlations.
